title: 1 Samuel 11:1–11
context: 1 Samuel 11:1–11 tells how Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh Gilead and offers terms that would gouge out every right eye as a disgrace to all Israel. The elders ask for seven days to seek a rescuer. When the news reaches Gibeah, God’s Spirit comes mightily on Saul, the newly anointed but not yet proven king (10:1, 24–27). He summons Israel by sending pieces of a yoke of oxen, the dread of the LORD falls on the people, and Saul routs the Ammonites at dawn. Some ancient manuscripts, including a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel, contain an additional paragraph about Nahash before 11:1, which some modern translations include and the WEB does not. Both traditions read the passage as God raising up deliverance through Saul in a way that echoes the judges.

verses.text: Then Nahash the Ammonite came up and encamped against Jabesh Gilead; and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh Gilead, and its men offer to serve him if he makes a covenant with them. Arminian readers see a town so weak that it is ready to surrender, and they note that Israel’s lack of unity under the judges left outlying towns exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe that the crisis tests the newly chosen king (10:24–27). Both traditions note the textual question about the longer opening found in a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel and agree that the main story is the same in either form.

verses.text: Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “On this condition I will make it with you, that all your right eyes be gouged out. I will make this dishonor all Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Nahash agrees only if every right eye is gouged out as a disgrace to all Israel. Arminian readers see the cruelty of the oppressor, whose terms aim at humiliating the whole nation and disabling the men for battle, not only at conquering one town.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the insult is directed at Israel as a whole, and therefore at Israel’s God. Both traditions read the verse as setting up a crisis that calls for deliverance and exposes Israel’s need for God-given leadership.

verses.text: The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Give us seven days, that we may send messengers to all the borders of Israel; and then, if there is no one to save us, we will come out to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The elders ask for seven days to send messengers through Israel, promising to surrender if no one saves them. Arminian readers see the elders seeking help from their fellow Israelites, and note the uncertainty about whether anyone will respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Nahash’s granting of the delay may reflect contempt for Israel’s ability to respond. Both traditions see the seven days as heightening the suspense and setting the stage for God to act through Saul.

verses.text: Then the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, and spoke these words in the ears of the people, then all the people lifted up their voice and wept.
verses.arminianNotes: The messengers come to Gibeah of Saul, and the people weep aloud. Arminian readers note that the people’s first response is grief rather than action, which shows how helpless they feel without a leader to rally them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that Gibeah is Saul’s hometown, so the news comes straight to the new king. Both traditions read the weeping as a sign of Israel’s weakness that God is about to answer.

verses.text: Behold, Saul came following the oxen out of the field; and Saul said, “What ails the people that they weep?” They told him the words of the men of Jabesh.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul comes in from the field behind the oxen and asks why the people are weeping. Arminians see humility in Saul, still working his farm after being anointed, and see God’s call finding him in ordinary work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the parallel with Gideon threshing (Judges 6:11) and other leaders called from daily work. Both traditions read the scene as showing that Saul’s kingship has not yet been proven, setting up the Spirit’s empowering in the next verse.

verses.text: God’s Spirit came mightily on Saul when he heard those words, and his anger burned hot.
verses.arminianNotes: God’s Spirit comes mightily on Saul when he hears the news, and his anger burns hot. Arminian readers see the Spirit equipping Saul for a specific task, and they note that later chapters show that such empowering did not guarantee Saul’s lasting faithfulness (16:14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the Spirit’s coming here is an empowering for leadership like that given to the judges (Judges 14:6), not a statement about Saul’s regeneration. Both traditions see the anger as righteous indignation at the threat against God’s people.

verses.text: He took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces, then sent them throughout all the borders of Israel by the hand of messengers, saying, “Whoever doesn’t come out after Saul and after Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen.” The dread of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out as one man.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul cuts up a yoke of oxen and sends the pieces through Israel, warning that the oxen of anyone who does not follow will be treated the same way. The dread of the LORD falls on the people. Arminians see God working through Saul’s bold summons to move the people to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the text credits the response to the dread of the LORD. Many interpreters note the echo of the Levite’s grim summons in Judges 19:29, now used for deliverance. Both traditions see the unity of "one man" as God’s work.

verses.text: He counted them in Bezek; and the children of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul counts the troops at Bezek: three hundred thousand of Israel and thirty thousand of Judah. Arminians see the size of the response as evidence that the people answered God’s call through Saul, a reversal of the scattered response seen in the days of the judges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Large numbers in Samuel are discussed by interpreters, since the Hebrew word for "thousand" may sometimes mean a military unit. Both traditions note the separate count for Judah, which anticipates the later division of the kingdom.

verses.text: They said to the messengers who came, “Tell the men of Jabesh Gilead, ‘Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be rescued.’ ” The messengers came and told the men of Jabesh; and they were glad.
verses.arminianNotes: The army sends word to Jabesh that they will be rescued tomorrow by the time the sun is hot, and the men of Jabesh rejoice. Arminian readers see the promise of deliverance turning despair into joy, a pattern of God’s saving help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe that the promise is specific and confident. Both traditions read the message as part of a careful account of how God delivered Jabesh, which the town remembered when it later honored Saul at his death (31:11–13).

verses.text: Therefore the men of Jabesh said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us all that seems good to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Jabesh tell Nahash that tomorrow they will come out and he may do with them as he likes. Arminian readers see a wise use of words that keeps Nahash off guard while help is coming, without stating anything about the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the words are ambiguous: they sound like surrender but set up the Ammonites’ defeat. Both traditions read the verse as part of the story’s suspense rather than as a statement of moral approval of deception.

verses.text: On the next day, Saul put the people in three companies; and they came into the middle of the camp in the morning watch, and struck the Ammonites until the heat of the day. Those who remained were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul divides the army into three companies, attacks in the morning watch, and strikes the Ammonites until the heat of the day, scattering the survivors. Arminians see Saul’s leadership and courage displayed, with God giving victory through his obedient action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the victory fulfills the promise of 11:9 and that Saul himself credits it to the LORD in 11:13. Both traditions see God using a leader’s skill and courage to deliver his people.
